Jozi Cats - Africa's first gay rugby club

By: Sophia Phirippides | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Paragons or pariahs? Are South Africans ready to embrace homosexual role models in sport? Africa's first gay and inclusive ruby club, Jozi Cats, is setting the trend for change.

Summary:
Jozi Cats, Africa’s first gay and inclusive rugby club, in May this year launched a provocative recruitment campaign that made headlines across the world, turning typical homosexual slurs on their head like, "fairy, "pansy", "pillow biter" and "fudge packer". The campaign created a stir beyond our borders, breaking the silence and taboo around homosexuality in sport. They are unashamedly embracing their their gayness and love of rugby at the same time, as well as raising the question of why there should even be a need for such a club in this day and age?

“The truth of the matter is that many of our players don’t feel like they can be openly gay and be a rugby player in South Africa,” says Kuni. “So we started Jozi Cats as a space where they could be both. The club is somewhere that players can play social and competitive rugby in a safe and non-judgmental environment.

”The poignant campaign also helps to smash perceptions that gay men fit a certain stereotype which has been formed by society, which is why it was so crucial to use players from the club in the poster campaign.

Carte Blanche meets some of these brave young men and goes behind the scenes in what is not your typical day at the rugby, as we explore the underlying stereotype of the "macho" sportsman and we meet some of the men behind the posters.

Further information:
Last year South African rugby player Jacques Potgieter was fined 20 000 Australian dollars for a derogatory slur aimed at two Brumbies players. He apologised publicly for the use of the word "faggot" and said he meant no malice and it was a wrong of him to do so. But for some it was not enough, he did not aplogise to the people he had offended, which was the LGBTQI community.

There have been other sportsmen around the world who have been prejudiced for "coming out". An anonymous footballer "Nico" who played for the Bundasliga, came out after midfielder Thomas Hitzlsperger "came out" as he thought it would make it easier for him, but he found out that it only became worse. In the locker rooms he found his team mates now showering with shorts on, and later he was dropped as apparently, he did not have a "good" season.

Rhyian Anderson-Morley, an Aussie Rules player, revealed in a column in 2014 that his sexuality nearly forced him to give up sport because he felt so shackled by what he might be perceived to be like. He eventually came out publicly in a column for The Age Newspaper and says he’s training better than ever.

"Attitudes towards homosexuality vary greatly from country to country and things are pretty tough in Africa with 38 countries criminalising homosexuality. South Africa has been one of the most progressive countries on the continent and, in a way, in the world, but homophobia has by no means gone away.

An Afrobarometer survey recently found that 23% of South Africans “aren’t tolerant” of homosexuals. While South Africa was the second most tolerant of all countries surveyed and expressed tolerance levels significantly higher than the 79% across the continent, corrective rape of women and hate crimes against men, especially in rural communities, are deeply troubling issues which we have not even begun to tackle adequately."

Chris Verrijd, who is the PR behind the campaign, says he can't wait for the day, when a South African rugby player has the courage to "come out" while he is still active in the sport. He believes South Africa needs role models who can break down the stereotypes in a typical sporting culture which is often dominated by outdated "macho" and"Jock" attitudes.

“I think if you look at other players who have come out, then yes, definitely we’re ready for a gay Springbok. Because it’s all about skill and that’s what it’s always been about, we want players to be appreciated for their skill and not be defined by their sexuality,” Kuni says.

If the Jozi Cats have their way, that player might even come from their club. They have partnered with the Wanderers Rugby Club which allows them access to some great facilities and the potential for talented players to make the step up to the Golden Lions.

These are just ordinary guys who love to play rugby, but happen to be gay. They are also one of the few clubs who teach adults to play rugby, and you don't have to be gay to play for them.

We live in a progressive society and yet very often homosexuality is condemned as "abnormal". A high profile homosexual role model can break down these perceptions and pave the way to a greater understanding of homosexuality within society. Young men who may be battling with questions around their sexuality may lose some of the fear that surrounds this taboo.

"The club is acutely aware that not everyone is ready to come out to the world yet and all they want to do is foster a safe environment for people of all sexualities. But it has big dreams, too. The clubs is firmly focused on representing South Africa at global Gay Rugby level and even the Gay Games."

Jozi Cats is about having fun and being able to be yourself and enjoy your rugby, but in the greater context, it is creating a way forward where the question around homosexuality in sport can be raised and brought to public awareness and possibly in the not too distant future homophobia around sport will not be an issue and being yourself and a good sportsman will simply be enough.

Press Release:


Jozi Cats
Are South Africans ready to embrace homosexual role models in sport? Jozi Cats, Africa’s first gay and inclusive rugby club, is setting the trend for change. Carte Blanche goes behind the scenes to meet the men determined to challenge stereotypes and find out why there is a need for a club like Jozi Cats in South Africa.


Script:


Carte Blanche – Jozi Cats Script Final.

Audio
Teveshan:



Waking up at seven o clock on a Saturday morning, be at practice at eight,

It's quite gruelling

Just because you're forced to be at that fitness level

It's a whole different kind of mental preparation, you kind of go into that big match temperament mode

Link: Teveshan Kuni may seem just like an ordinary rugby player who is passionate about the sport, but he belongs to an extraordinary team, Jozi Cats, Africa's first gay and inclusive Rugby club.

Teveshan: It's considered such a macho sport that people just go like, gay guys don't play rugby, come meet some guys in my team and they good rugby players.

VO: Jozi Cats made it's name earlier this year by launching a recruitment campaign for their Rugby Club, that reverberated around the world. Typical homosexual slurs were parodied like: Pansy, fairy, Queen and Flamer

Chris: Teveshan approached us in the beginning, look we need help we've started this rugby club but kind of interest has plateaued help us. So i thought about it, and said to him, let me speak to my CEO, so I walked into her office and said, there's this gay rugby team... she said do it.

VO: Chris Verrijdt of Havas PR South Africa, knew that Jozi Cats had no money to make a real impact, but he and his team were faced with the challenge to recruit players.

Chris: So we went onto Facebook and he said to me well they don't even look gay, i said well, exactly, thats kind of when the idea hit me.

VO: They looked at 150 gay slurs and whittled them down to 6 with the final poster pay off line “Rugby that's so Gay.”

Anthony: What do people think when they hear of gay rugby players, they laugh hence the genius behind the campaign, in terms of challenging gay stereo types, as well as homophobia in sport.

VO:

When Anthony Seger became one of the faces of Jozi Cats, he says it was scary at first, but he found it cathartic and liberating.

Anthony: I mean I'm imortalised on the internet for the rest of my life which is fantastic because it serves a purpose and a point.

Chris: I stressed throughout the process that we would be consulting them, because some of the guys hadn't come out yet there were terms that would be associated with the players in those shots for the rest of their lives.

Nathi: I'm a better person with being out to all my work colleagues, there's been support all round.

VO: Nathi Khoza and poster boy “Pansy”, is a sports co-ordinator at a primary school and one of the coaches and founders of Jozi Cats.

Nathi: Having played in high school and playing at first team level, there's a change room banter, which makes someone that's closeted feel uncomfortable and not safe, so to be offered an opportunity to be part of an environment where you dont have to explain yourself that was a huge bonus.

VO: The campaign was simple, imagery with captions that challenged stereotypes. When they put it out into the world, they had an inkling that it would cause a reaction and possibly spark a conversation but Jozi Cats had no idea how big it would become.

Teveshan: We've been seen in over like 140 countries, apparently about 350 million people world wide, this is a viral campaign that just went ballistic.

Chris: When you start putting it into context that we were able to say what people around the world weren't able to say, that's when we started really seeing the importance of a campaign like this

Link: It's pretty tough to be gay in Africa with 38 countries criminalising homosexuality, but South Africa is one of the most progressive countries in the world when it comes to LGBTQI rights, still are we ready to have a gay sports hero?

Vox Pop: Idealistically speaking, we'd like to say we're ready, but we're not ready.



Vox Pop, Kobus Raiders Rugby player:

(Afrikaans) Rugby is a man's sport, if he turns out to be like that, then that's his choice. Everyone plays rugby to enjoy it, so it's his choice and rugby is actually for everyone, there are girls that play rugby.


Vox Pop:

It's a bit of a paradigm shift but it will get there hopefully, you know, I don't think we're ready as yet

VO: This is what some straight rugby players had to say when we asked them the tough question, but in the greater context of sport it hasn't been easy for sporting heroes to embrace their sexual orientation openly. Even Gareth Thomas Captain of Wales, and the British Lions, only had the courage to come out at the end of his career.

Chris:
We know that there is homophobia in sport and thats probably one of the driving factors about why Jozi Cats was established.


VO: It hasn't all been a joy ride for Jozi Cats, they had to face the impact of some negative responses

Chris: Everything from you should die, you are all paedophiles, you should all be HIV positive. But was was incredible in that environment again it was the other followers, that started defending us and they then started having the conversation.

VO: So the big question is, do they have what it takes to play rugby with the Big Guns?

Anthony: Since the campaign we've had so many phenomenal players rock up we're getting better and better, we're beating teams now, that we weren't beating at the beginning of the league.

VOX POP: We already played them before, not knowing obviously the nuances that it's a gay team, but ja the gents were full of fun.

Nathi: We expect our players to perform at the same level as other club rugby players we've had broken fingers and ja we're pretty much like any other rugby team

Teveshan: We play in the conventional leagues we just a normal rugby club, some of the players happen to be gay, bisexual or identify as transgender male.

VO: And some South African rugby players and fans don't seem too non plussed over the issue.. after all...

VOX POP Kobus: Rugby is Rugby, and I don't mind if he's gay.

Anthony: We are also an affiliate club to Wanderers, and who knows maybe we will be a feed through or a channel for the next Springbok, that perhaps wouldn't have gotten the opportunity because of his sexual identity.






PROMO 15”:

Claire Link:

Start with a few shots if rugby

This may seem like an ordinary day at the rugby with players passionate about the sport, but Jozi Cats is not what you would call a regular rugby team, it's Africa's first gay and inclusive rugby Club.
End with poster – Rugby that's so Gay




PROMO 15”:


VO:

Jozi Cats rugby club, Paragons or Pariahs.. or does it really matter?

Teveshan:

We play in the conventional leagues, we just a normal rugby club, some of the players happen to be gay, bisexual or identify as transgender male.


PROMO 10”

Claire Link:

Catch our fixture, it's rough, it's tough, it's the Jozi Cats, one of the most controversial rugby teams on the continent – Rugby that's so gay.

Anthony: Since the campaign we've had so many phenomenal players rock up we're getting better and better, we're beating teams now, that we weren't beating at the beginning of the league. VOX POP: We already played them before, not knowing obviously the nuances that it's a gay team, but ja the gents were full of fun. Nathi: We expect our players to perform at the same level as other club rugby players we've had broken fingers and ja we're pretty much like any other rugby team Teveshan: We play in the conventional leagues we just a normal rugby club, some of the players happen to be gay, bisexual or identify as transgender male. VO: And some South African rugby players and fans don't seem too non plussed over the issue.. after all... VOX POP Kobus: Rugby is Rugby, and I don't mind if he's gay. Anthony: We are also an affiliate club to Wanderers, and who knows maybe we will be a feed through or a channel for the next Springbok, that perhaps wouldn't have gotten the opportunity because of his sexual identity. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Paragons or pariahs? Are South Africans ready to embrace homosexual role models in sport? Africa's first gay and inclusive ruby club, Jozi Cats, is setting the trend for change.
metadata.Summary: Jozi Cats, Africa’s first gay and inclusive rugby club, in May this year launched a provocative recruitment campaign that made headlines across the world, turning typical homosexual slurs on their head like, "fairy, "pansy", "pillow biter" and "fudge packer". The campaign created a stir beyond our borders, breaking the silence and taboo around homosexuality in sport. They are unashamedly embracing their their gayness and love of rugby at the same time, as well as raising the question of why there should even be a need for such a club in this day and age? “The truth of the matter is that many of our players don’t feel like they can be openly gay and be a rugby player in South Africa,” says Kuni. “So we started Jozi Cats as a space where they could be both. The club is somewhere that players can play social and competitive rugby in a safe and non-judgmental environment. ”The poignant campaign also helps to smash perceptions that gay men fit a certain stereotype which has been formed by society, which is why it was so crucial to use players from the club in the poster campaign. Carte Blanche meets some of these brave young men and goes behind the scenes in what is not your typical day at the rugby, as we explore the underlying stereotype of the "macho" sportsman and we meet some of the men behind the posters.
metadata.Further information: Last year South African rugby player Jacques Potgieter was fined 20 000 Australian dollars for a derogatory slur aimed at two Brumbies players. He apologised publicly for the use of the word "faggot" and said he meant no malice and it was a wrong of him to do so. But for some it was not enough, he did not aplogise to the people he had offended, which was the LGBTQI community. There have been other sportsmen around the world who have been prejudiced for "coming out". An anonymous footballer "Nico" who played for the Bundasliga, came out after midfielder Thomas Hitzlsperger "came out" as he thought it would make it easier for him, but he found out that it only became worse. In the locker rooms he found his team mates now showering with shorts on, and later he was dropped as apparently, he did not have a "good" season. Rhyian Anderson-Morley, an Aussie Rules player, revealed in a column in 2014 that his sexuality nearly forced him to give up sport because he felt so shackled by what he might be perceived to be like. He eventually came out publicly in a column for The Age Newspaper and says he’s training better than ever. "Attitudes towards homosexuality vary greatly from country to country and things are pretty tough in Africa with 38 countries criminalising homosexuality. South Africa has been one of the most progressive countries on the continent and, in a way, in the world, but homophobia has by no means gone away. An Afrobarometer survey recently found that 23% of South Africans “aren’t tolerant” of homosexuals. While South Africa was the second most tolerant of all countries surveyed and expressed tolerance levels significantly higher than the 79% across the continent, corrective rape of women and hate crimes against men, especially in rural communities, are deeply troubling issues which we have not even begun to tackle adequately." Chris Verrijd, who is the PR behind the campaign, says he can't wait for the day, when a South African rugby player has the courage to "come out" while he is still active in the sport. He believes South Africa needs role models who can break down the stereotypes in a typical sporting culture which is often dominated by outdated "macho" and"Jock" attitudes. “I think if you look at other players who have come out, then yes, definitely we’re ready for a gay Springbok. Because it’s all about skill and that’s what it’s always been about, we want players to be appreciated for their skill and not be defined by their sexuality,” Kuni says. If the Jozi Cats have their way, that player might even come from their club. They have partnered with the Wanderers Rugby Club which allows them access to some great facilities and the potential for talented players to make the step up to the Golden Lions. These are just ordinary guys who love to play rugby, but happen to be gay. They are also one of the few clubs who teach adults to play rugby, and you don't have to be gay to play for them. We live in a progressive society and yet very often homosexuality is condemned as "abnormal". A high profile homosexual role model can break down these perceptions and pave the way to a greater understanding of homosexuality within society. Young men who may be battling with questions around their sexuality may lose some of the fear that surrounds this taboo. "The club is acutely aware that not everyone is ready to come out to the world yet and all they want to do is foster a safe environment for people of all sexualities. But it has big dreams, too. The clubs is firmly focused on representing South Africa at global Gay Rugby level and even the Gay Games." Jozi Cats is about having fun and being able to be yourself and enjoy your rugby, but in the greater context, it is creating a way forward where the question around homosexuality in sport can be raised and brought to public awareness and possibly in the not too distant future homophobia around sport will not be an issue and being yourself and a good sportsman will simply be enough.
